title: The Pharisees
lead: A Jewish movement of the late Second Temple period, known for careful keeping of the law, including purity, tithing and the Sabbath, and for the "traditions of the elders" that interpreted it. They are Jesus' most frequent debate partners in the Gospels; Paul was one, and the later rabbis saw them as their forerunners.

sections.b: Josephus describes the Pharisees as one of three main Jewish "schools," alongside the Sadducees and Essenes. He says they were admired by ordinary people, held to the traditions of the fathers, and believed in the resurrection and in God's providence alongside human choice. The name probably means "separated ones." Most were not priests but laymen, and they were not a ruling body, though some sat on councils. After the temple fell in AD 70, rabbis who carried on much of their approach shaped later Judaism.

The Gospels show Pharisees debating Jesus over the Sabbath, purity, fasting, divorce and his authority; Matthew's portrait is the sharpest (Matthew 23). Many scholars think Matthew's harsh tone reflects conflicts between his community and the synagogue leaders of his own day, after AD 70. The Gospels also show friendlier Pharisees (Luke 13:31; John 3:1–2; Acts 5:34). Christians have often used "Pharisee" as a word for hypocrite, which many Jewish and Christian scholars today warn is unfair to the historical movement.
